title: Imperfect Women
synopsis: Eleanor was your best friend for twenty years. She's been murdered. You and Mary, the third friend, each know exactly half of the secret that killed her. You have to decide whether to tell each other.

nodes.text: Mary calls at 6:14 a.m. crying. You sit on the edge of the bed and hear the sentence 'Eleanor is dead' and your husband, beside you, does not yet know. The clock keeps moving.

choices.text: Wake your husband
choices.consequence: You choose to wake your husband. It opens the route to His Reaction, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Get dressed and go to Mary immediately
choices.consequence: You commit to get dressed and go to Mary immediately. By Mary's Kitchen, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Your husband Robert reacts in a way that is one ratchet off from what you expected. He is sad. He is also, in a way you can't name, alert. The distance between The Affair Half and The Money Half begins with the choice between “Notice the alertness” and “Ignore it; he loved Eleanor.”

choices.text: Notice the alertness
choices.consequence: You notice the alertness. The decision moves you toward The Affair Half and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Ignore it; he loved Eleanor
choices.consequence: You ignore it; he loved Eleanor. The decision moves you toward The Money Half and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Mary, at her counter, hands you a coffee with the same chip in the mug she's had since college. She says, before you can speak, 'I knew about Eleanor and someone. “Ask her who she suspected” draws you toward The Affair Half; “Tell her your half first” leaves The Money Half waiting on the other side.

choices.text: Ask her who she suspected
choices.consequence: You ask her who she suspected. The decision moves you toward The Affair Half and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Tell her your half first
choices.consequence: You commit to tell her your half first. By The Money Half, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Eleanor had been having an affair for the last year. You knew because she told you. You don't know with whom. Mary, you suspect, knew the man's name but didn't know it was Eleanor. “Tell Mary the affair half now” draws you toward The Detective; “Wait to see what Mary volunteers” leaves The Husband, Nathan waiting on the other side.

choices.text: Tell Mary the affair half now
choices.consequence: You commit to tell Mary the affair half now. By The Detective, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

choices.text: Wait to see what Mary volunteers
choices.consequence: You choose to wait to see what Mary volunteers. It opens the route to The Husband, Nathan, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Eleanor had been managing money — yours, Mary's, hers — and you'd noticed a discrepancy two months ago. You'd been planning to ask her about it the day she died. The half-secret is, somehow, becoming whole. The paths divide here: “Tell Mary about the money” leads into The Detective, while “Hold the money for now; the affair feels closer to motive” makes The Husband, Nathan the next reckoning.

choices.text: Tell Mary about the money
choices.consequence: You choose to tell Mary about the money. It opens the route to The Detective, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Hold the money for now; the affair feels closer to motive
choices.consequence: You hold the money for now; the affair feels closer to motive. The decision moves you toward The Husband, Nathan and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Detective Kapoor is kind, careful, slow. She asks you both about Eleanor's life in the past year. She has noticed, you can tell, the small inconsistency between your accounts. Choose “Trust her with the affair half” and The Daughter comes into view; choose “Trust her with the money half” and the road bends toward Robert, Out.

choices.text: Trust her with the affair half
choices.consequence: You choose to trust her with the affair half. It opens the route to The Daughter, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Trust her with the money half
choices.consequence: You commit to trust her with the money half. By Robert, Out, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Eleanor's husband Nathan sits in his kitchen looking smaller than you remember. He says he didn't know about the affair. He says it twice. He looks at you the second time. The paths divide here: “Believe him” leads into The Daughter, while “Watch him more closely” makes Robert, Out the next reckoning.

choices.text: Believe him
choices.consequence: You believe him. The decision moves you toward The Daughter and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Watch him more closely
choices.consequence: You commit to watch him more closely. By Robert, Out, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Eleanor's seventeen-year-old, Sophie, asks you, in the back garden, if you knew her mother was unhappy. You realize, again, that 'mother' and 'friend' are different people you each knew. “Tell Sophie what you knew” draws you toward The Photo; “Tell Sophie that her mother loved her” leaves Mary's Husband waiting on the other side.

choices.text: Tell Sophie what you knew
choices.consequence: You tell Sophie what you knew. The decision moves you toward The Photo and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Tell Sophie that her mother loved her
choices.consequence: Lead with the kindest truth. You choose to tell Sophie that her mother loved her. It opens the route to Mary's Husband, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Your husband Robert is, conveniently, out late three nights running. He says it's work. The shoes by the door, when he comes home, are wet. It hasn't rained. The paths divide here: “Follow Robert one night” leads into The Photo, while “Ask Mary if she's noticed the same about her husband” makes Mary's Husband the next reckoning.

choices.text: Follow Robert one night
choices.consequence: You commit to follow Robert one night. By The Photo, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

choices.text: Ask Mary if she's noticed the same about her husband
choices.consequence: You commit to ask Mary if she's noticed the same about her husband. By Mary's Husband, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: On Eleanor's phone, recovered after a week, is a photo of a hotel-room ceiling. The angle is innocuous to anyone who doesn't know the ceiling. You know the ceiling. Choose “Tell Mary you recognize the ceiling” and The Garage Conversation comes into view; choose “Tell Detective Kapoor” and the road bends toward Detective Kapoor's Case.

choices.text: Tell Mary you recognize the ceiling
choices.consequence: You tell Mary you recognize the ceiling. The decision moves you toward The Garage Conversation and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Tell Detective Kapoor
choices.consequence: You commit to tell Detective Kapoor. By Detective Kapoor's Case, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Mary, slowly, admits that her husband Tom has been distant for months. Tom and Robert and Nathan all go to the same gym. The gym is, you realize, three suburbs away from any of their homes.

choices.text: Plan to confront the husbands together
choices.consequence: You choose to plan to confront the husbands together. It opens the route to The Garage Conversation, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Each speak to your own first
choices.consequence: You choose to each speak to your own first. It opens the route to Detective Kapoor's Case, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: You and Mary corner Robert and Tom in Robert's garage on a Saturday morning. The truth comes out in stages — yes, an affair, no, with one of them, no, neither knew Eleanor would be killed.

choices.text: Believe the parts that exonerate them
choices.consequence: You believe the parts that exonerate them. The decision moves you toward The Arrest and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Disbelieve until proven
choices.consequence: Marriage is also evidence. You commit to disbelieve until proven. By The Marriage Counseling, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Kapoor calls you in for a quiet meeting. She has, she says, narrowed it. She tells you a name. The name is on neither half of your secret. The room moves. “Help her gather what she needs” draws you toward The Arrest; “Take a breath before responding” leaves The Marriage Counseling waiting on the other side.

choices.text: Help her gather what she needs
choices.consequence: You help her gather what she needs. The decision moves you toward The Arrest and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Take a breath before responding
choices.consequence: You commit to take a breath before responding. By The Marriage Counseling, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: An arrest is made. The killer is, almost mundanely, a stranger Eleanor had been planning to leave the marriage for — and who had been planning, in his own ugly way, to leave her too. The motive is small and the loss is enormous.

choices.text: Attend the trial through to verdict
choices.consequence: You commit to attend the trial through to verdict. By Mary and You, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

choices.text: Step back; protect your own family
choices.consequence: You choose to step back; protect your own family. It opens the route to Your Daughter, Listening, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: You and Robert sit with a therapist for the first time in your marriage. The truth about his Tuesdays comes out. It is not an affair. It is a less interesting and more painful answer: he has been visiting a sponsor at AA.

choices.text: Apologize fully
choices.consequence: You commit to apologize fully. By Mary and You, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

choices.text: Ask why he kept it secret
choices.consequence: Repair requires questions. You ask why he kept it secret. The decision moves you toward Your Daughter, Listening and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Mary and you, after, walk every Sunday for a year. You don't talk about Eleanor every walk. You talk about her enough. The friendship that was three is, slowly, two. The two is, sometimes, enough.

choices.text: Make Sundays a permanent ritual
choices.consequence: You choose to make Sundays a permanent ritual. It opens the route to Sophie's University, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Bring Sophie sometimes
choices.consequence: Three again, differently. You commit to bring Sophie sometimes. By The Anniversary, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Your own daughter, fifteen, asks you to teach her how to be a friend like you are friends. You sit on the porch and try to think of an answer that isn't a Hallmark card.

choices.text: Model that for her with your own friends
choices.consequence: You choose to model that for her with your own friends. It opens the route to Sophie's University, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Send her to call her best friend now
choices.consequence: You send her to call her best friend now. The decision moves you toward The Anniversary and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Sophie's university acceptance arrives on a Tuesday. You and Mary throw her a party. She gives a small speech and thanks you both. You realize, with a feeling that is both grief and gratitude, that Eleanor is in this room.

choices.text: Tell Sophie about her mother's good qualities
choices.consequence: You choose to tell Sophie about her mother's good qualities. It opens the route to The Photograph on the Wall, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Sit beside Mary and just let it be
choices.consequence: You sit beside Mary and just let it be. The decision moves you toward The Photograph on the Wall and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: One year after Eleanor died you and Mary and Nathan and Sophie all eat dinner at the same restaurant Eleanor loved. The food is fine. The night is full of stories you'd forgotten. You laugh more than you cry. Eleanor would, you realize, approve.

choices.text: Make this the new tradition
choices.consequence: You choose to make this the new tradition. It opens the route to The Photograph on the Wall, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Let it be a one-time thing
choices.consequence: Some moments belong to once. You commit to let it be a one-time thing. By The Photograph on the Wall, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Years on, you stop at a photograph of the three of you from a college trip. You realize you don't flinch anymore. You realize you can hold both sadness and gratitude in the same hand. You choose what to do with that hand next.

choices.text: Hand it to Sophie
choices.consequence: You hand it to Sophie. The decision moves you toward Sophie's Aunts and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Keep it on your own wall and call Mary
choices.consequence: You keep it on your own wall and call Mary. The decision moves you toward Sunday Walks and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: You and Mary become Sophie's aunts in a real, unofficial way. You attend her graduation. You attend her wedding. At her wedding she names a child after Eleanor. You both cry without performing it. The road into Sophie's Aunts began with “Hand it to Sophie” in The Photograph on the Wall; here, that decision stops being a moment and becomes a life.

You and Mary walk for the next thirty years. You bury parents and welcome grandchildren. You speak of Eleanor often, then less often, then often again in the way grief loops. The friendship, in the end, is the answer to the question her death almost asked.
